text: The euphoria in the American ranks from the Eutaw Springs battle soon evaporated, and Greene had his hands full dealing with a sick, hungry, and discontented army. Greene responded by using patriot patrols to watch the British while he marched his Continentals back to their habitual campsite along the Santee River. Meanwhile, Greene did what he could to shape operations in Virginia and North Carolina and worked on prisoner exchanges with Leslie. At the same time, his officers nursed the army back to health and prepared to resume the campaign in cooler weather. Greene received welcome news in late October when he learned of General Cornwallis’s surrender at Yorktown. Soon thereafter, Greene received an offer from Leslie to resume prisoner exchanges—an offer Greene spurned over his resentment of Isaac Hayne’s execution. Greene also learned that the Continental Congress had voted their thanks to the individual units and particular officers for the Eutaw Springs battle. Congress especially honored Greene with the award of a gold medal commemorating what they saw as a victory at Eutaw Springs.

Cornwallis’s surrender did nothing to change matters in North America immediately (Map 8). Clinton still commanded 15,000 combat troops in New York alone, and the British army and Royal Navy had substantial combat forces in the West Indies. Within the southern theater, the British still controlled roughly 9,000 British regulars and provincials, and hundreds more loyalist supporters. Hardcore loyalists continued to launch raids from Charleston and Savannah, and in several instances, they inflicted heavy losses on isolated rebel patrols. However, the surrender at Yorktown demoralized the British troops so much that their commanders refused to continue risking troops in unnecessary offensive operations. Greene led a reconnaissance force toward Dorchester in November 1781, which encountered only scattered resistance from loyalist partisans, while General Leslie quietly withdrew the Dorchester garrison down to Charleston.
citation: Skinner, Harold Allen, Jr. The War in the Carolinas and Georgia, 1781–1782. U.S. Army Campaigns of the Revolutionary War, CMH Pub 71-52. Washington, D.C.: Center of Military History, United States Army, 2026.
title: The War in the Carolinas and Georgia
